Preprint — arXiv:2609.37143v1 [cs.SE]; no published venue stated

Fudan University; City University of Hong Kong; Chinese University of Hong Kong; Singapore Management University; HKUST (GZ); Monash University Malaysia; Harbin Institute of Technology; two independent researchers (Hong Kong) (mainly academic)

Proposes an evaluation method; secondary: Compares — LoLBench benchmark of 100 modular development tasks built from human-written enhancement proposals (EPs) on 29 large software systems, with EP–PR matching, system-level F2P/P2P tests augmented by mutation- and coverage-guided generation, and section-level scoring; 28 agents (6 models × 5 scaffolds) compared, plus an EP-vs-specification comparison for three agents

No SDD approach evaluated. Scaffolds: Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Pi, mini-SWE-agent (versions not stated). Models via OpenRouter at second-highest reasoning effort: DeepSeek V4 Flash, Opus 5, Kimi K3, GPT-5.6 Sol, GLM-5.2, MiniMax M3 (Codex + Opus 5 and Claude Code + GPT-5.6 Sol unavailable). Input variants: EP only (main) vs EP reformulated as a specification with a reference-derived file tree and API specification (NL2Repo-Bench instruction format), for three agents

Agent receives a human-written enhancement proposal (PEP, JEP, KIP, FLIP, KEP, RFC, NEP etc.; about 5,000 words with user intent and high-level design; test plan and validation sections removed) and the pre-implementation codebase; must deliver solution.patch (tests optional in test.patch). Specification variant adds a file tree and API specification derived from the reference solution. Task bundle in Harbor format: instructions.md, task.toml, environment/, solution/, tests/

Agent run in an offline Harbor sandbox (six-hour limit, terminated after one hour without progress); verifier runs F2P and P2P tests. Agent activity classified into requirement understanding, task planning, code localization, code editing, code verification, plus repair loops. Benchmark construction: (I) project collection, (II) EP–PR matching with 28 static and 8 semantic rules, LLM-judge quality ranking (score ≥ 8.0) and expert review, (III) task construction with F2P/P2P tests in Docker, (IV) task enhancement with proposal mutants and mutation- and coverage-guided F2P test generation, section–test mapping
None during agent runs. In construction, final expert review of each EP–PR candidate after validation and LLM ranking; generated tests audited
N/A (no SDD approach); agents implement a proposal end to end in an existing large codebase

Not classifiable (no SDD approach evaluated). Authors' wording: 'perception capability of grounding user intent and high-level design to derive a specification'; 'current agents perform substantially better on specifications than on abstract proposals'
Existing code base (modular development: implementing enhancement proposals in large existing software systems)

100 tasks from 29 systems; proposals about 5,000 words; repositories mean 2,393.6k source LoC (median 1,545.1k); reference PRs mean 5,499 changed LoC (median 2,774), 64.9 files / 40.1 classes / 195.9 functions modified; 7.3% of target class names mentioned in proposals

Five domains: compilers (48 tasks, e.g. CPython, OpenJDK, Rust, TypeScript), data science (29, e.g. Apache Flink, Kafka, NumPy), distributed systems (17, e.g. Kubernetes, Prometheus), databases (3), web frameworks (3)

Automatic: Harbor verifier runs hidden F2P and P2P tests; turns, time, tokens and cost from trajectories. Failure analysis: predefined rules for observable modes plus an outcome-blinded LLM judge (GPT-5.6 Luna, pro reasoning, temperature 0) for requirement understanding and planning. Augmented tests generated by Codex + GPT-5.6 Sol and Claude Code + Opus 4.8

Tasks: 100 LoLBench tasks. Configurations: 28 model–scaffold agents; paired comparison of EP vs reference-derived specification for three agents. Baseline: none designated (specification variant compared against the EP results in Table 2). Held constant: tasks, offline Harbor sandbox, six-hour limit, second-highest reasoning effort, OpenRouter access, verifier. Acceptance tests: system-level F2P tests (original plus augmented) and P2P regression tests. Repetitions: one attempt per task and agent, retries only after provider or infrastructure failures. Human intervention: none

Best resolved 14% (Opus 5 with Claude Code and with mini-SWE-agent); mean 3.4%, median 2.0%; best completed 26.3% and F2P 52.7% (Claude Code + Opus 5). Opus 5 best under every scaffold supporting it. Variability across models is about 2.6× that across scaffolds (RSD 62.0% vs 24.0% for completed, 44.5% vs 17.3% for F2P). With Opus 5, mini-SWE-agent uses 3.2× the time, 5.0× the generated tokens and 2.8× the cost of Claude Code for the same 14 tasks. Code localization is the largest share of turns (60.4% initial, 44.2% repair) and of failure attribution (30.9 units), mostly missing cross-module context. Specifications raise resolved rate by 16–22 points (2.4–17×), max 34%. No significance tests

It separated models more than scaffolds and showed localization as the bottleneck, but resolved rates are low (median 2%), limiting discrimination at the bottom. Repeatability not assessed: one attempt per task. Limitations stated: functional correctness only; limited set of software systems; limited models and scaffolds and run-to-run variability not characterized; EPs may omit context from discussions; failure analysis relies partly on LLM judges

Limitations: evaluates only functional correctness (no maintainability or design conventions); tasks limited to well-maintained open-source communities with formal proposals; 28 agents only, one attempt per task; EPs omit surrounding discussion context, so some difficulty may come from incomplete specification; LLM-judge failure attribution is a diagnostic estimate. Gaps: agents struggle with perception (grounding abstract intent and design in large codebases, cross-module localization) as well as implementation; explicit implementation guidance removes much of the difficulty; future work on perception capability
